Stage 3 · Grammar

Three layers of one story

The background, the events, and what had already happened before them.

Read these four sentences from the recording.
  • He decided not to take the cable car down with his friends.
  • While he was looking for the path, he fell into a stream.
  • His phone wasn’t working because he had dropped it in the stream.
  • He had been at a barbecue restaurant on top of the mountain.
In the third sentence, which happened first — the phone stopping, or dropping it?
A story needs three past forms working together, not one.

When you tell a story in English, you are doing two things at once: reporting events, and telling your listener how those events relate to each other in time. The past simple alone can only do the first. The three narrative forms — past simple, past continuous and past perfect — exist so that you can do the second without adding explanations.

The past simple carries the story forward. Each past simple verb is one completed step: he decided, he fell, he broke his leg. If you tell everything in the order it happened, the past simple is all you need. The past continuous steps outside that chain to describe the background — something longer that was already in progress when an event happened. While he was looking for the path, he fell gives you the setting and the event in one sentence, and your listener knows immediately which is which.

The past perfect is the form that lets you break the chronological order safely. Sometimes you have to mention an earlier event later, usually to explain a cause: His phone didn’t work because he had dropped it in the stream. The dropping happened first, but you say it second. The past perfect is what stops that being confusing — it tells the listener ‘step back, this is before the point we have reached’.

That also explains when not to use it. If the order is already obvious, the past perfect adds nothing and makes the story heavy. He finished the meal and walked down the mountain needs no past perfect at all. Overusing this form is as much a mistake as omitting it, and it is a very common one in B1 writing.

Before you look at the table: the table below shows the three forms on a timeline rather than as a list. Look at where each one sits relative to the story’s main line; that picture is more useful than the endings.
One event, three layers
 Earlier→The moment→After
Past perfect
had + past participle		He had dropped his phone in the stream.    
Past continuous
was / were + -ing		  He was looking for the path.  
Past simple
-ed / irregular		  he fell into a stream and broke his leg.
FormIts job in a storyExample
Past simplethe events, one after another — this is the spine of the storyHe fell, broke his leg and tried to phone for help.
Past continuousthe longer background the events happen insideWhile he was walking down…
Past perfectsomething that had already finished before that moment…because he had dropped his phone.

The long one is interrupted by the short one. The past continuous sets the scene and the past simple cuts into it: While I was cooking, the lights went out. The reverse is almost never what you mean.

Use the past perfect only when the order matters. If you tell the events in the order they happened, the past simple is enough. The past perfect is for stepping back: The phone was dead. He had dropped it an hour earlier.

The mistake to avoid. Not While I was falling I broke my leg — falling is short, so it takes the past simple. Not After I had ate — the past perfect uses the past participle: had eaten.

One more. A finished time takes the past simple, not the present perfect recycled: I saw him last week, not I have seen him last week.

Full grammar reference — narrative forms — past simple, past continuous and past perfect

What it is

A story in English is built out of three past forms working together. The past simple carries the events that move the story forward. The past continuous sets the scene: a longer action already in progress when an event interrupts it. The past perfect steps further back, to something that had already happened before the point the story has reached.

What it means, and what it does

The three forms let you tell events out of order without confusing your listener. If you say He fell into a stream and broke his leg, the order of the words is the order of events. But He couldn’t phone for help because he had dropped his mobile in the stream puts an earlier event later in the sentence, and the past perfect is what makes that safe. The tense, not the word order, tells the listener what happened first.

When and why we use it

When you tell a story in English, you are doing two things at once: reporting events, and telling your listener how those events relate to each other in time. The past simple alone can only do the first. The three narrative forms — past simple, past continuous and past perfect — exist so that you can do the second without adding explanations.

The past simple carries the story forward. Each past simple verb is one completed step: he decided, he fell, he broke his leg. If you tell everything in the order it happened, the past simple is all you need. The past continuous steps outside that chain to describe the background — something longer that was already in progress when an event happened. While he was looking for the path, he fell gives you the setting and the event in one sentence, and your listener knows immediately which is which.

The past perfect is the form that lets you break the chronological order safely. Sometimes you have to mention an earlier event later, usually to explain a cause: His phone didn’t work because he had dropped it in the stream. The dropping happened first, but you say it second. The past perfect is what stops that being confusing — it tells the listener ‘step back, this is before the point we have reached’.

That also explains when not to use it. If the order is already obvious, the past perfect adds nothing and makes the story heavy. He finished the meal and walked down the mountain needs no past perfect at all. Overusing this form is as much a mistake as omitting it, and it is a very common one in B1 writing.

Typical situations

You need the narrative forms for any anecdote, personal story, news report, accident description or account of what happened at work — in speech and in writing. Every model narrative in this course uses all three.

  • The events of the story — completed actions in the order they happened; the backbone of any narrative.He decided to walk down, fell into a stream and broke his leg.
  • Background and setting — a longer action already going on when something happened; often after while or as.While he was looking for the path, he fell.
  • Two long actions at the same time — both in the continuous, usually joined by while.Teams of people were looking for him while he was lying in the stream.
  • Something that happened earlier — an event before the main past time, especially when you explain a cause.His phone didn’t work because he had dropped it in the water.
  • A state that reached back — how long something had been true at that past point.He had been at a barbecue restaurant on top of the mountain.
  • Interrupted plans — the past continuous for what was going on, the past simple for what stopped it.I was leaving the office when the phone rang.

How it differs from similar structures

Past simple = the whole event, seen as complete · past continuous = the middle of an action, not its beginning or end. I read the report (finished it) vs I was reading the report (in the middle of it).
Past simple = the event · past perfect = an event before that event. Only step back when the earlier event is told later.

How to build it

Past simple: subject + past form (regular: verb + -ed)
Past continuous: subject + was / were + verb-ing
Past perfect: subject + had + past participle
Past simple — affirmativeHe decided · They fell
Past simple — negativeHe didn’t decide — the main verb goes back to the base form.
Past simple — questionDid he decide…? · What did he do?
Past continuous — affirmativeI / he / she / it was looking · you / we / they were looking
Past continuous — negativeHe wasn’t looking · They weren’t looking
Past continuous — questionWas he looking…? · Were they looking…?
Past perfect — affirmativeHe had dropped it. · He’d dropped it.
Past perfect — negativeHe hadn’t brought any water.
Past perfect — questionHad he told anyone where he was going?
Short answersYes, he did. / No, they weren’t. / Yes, she had.

Spelling and word order

  • Regular past and past participle add -ed: walk → walked. After a silent -e, add only -d (decide → decided). Consonant + y becomes -ied (carry → carried). One stressed vowel + one consonant doubles it (stop → stopped, prefer → preferred).
  • -ing follows the same doubling rule: sit → sitting, travel → travelling (British) / traveling (American).
  • Irregular verbs must be learnt in threes, because the past simple and the past participle are often different: fall — fell — fallen, break — broke — broken, drink — drank — drunk, take — took — taken.

Saying it — contractions and stress

  • had is nearly always contracted to ’d in speech: he’d brought. This is why learners often do not hear the past perfect at all.
  • ’d can be had or would. The next word decides: he’d brought (past participle → had) but he’d bring (base form → would).
  • The -ed ending has three sounds: /t/ after voiceless sounds (walked), /d/ after voiced sounds (called), and /ɪd/ only after t or d (decided, wanted). It is not an extra syllable anywhere else.

Usage notes and exceptions

  • The past perfect is only needed when the order is not obvious. If you tell the events in the order they happened, the past simple alone is enough: He finished the meal and walked down. Overusing the past perfect is as much of an error as omitting it.
  • After when, both forms are possible and the meaning changes: When I arrived, they left (they left after I arrived) but When I arrived, they had left (they were already gone).
  • State verbs normally stay simple in the past too: He knew the path, not he was knowing.
  • Used to and would also describe the past, but for repeated habits rather than single events. They are the focus of Lesson 19.
  • Time expressions that force the past simple: yesterday, last week, in 2015, two days ago, then, after that. If one of these is present, the present perfect is wrong.

Watch out — the mistakes learners really make

  • While he looked for the path, he fell. → While he was looking for the path, he fell.While introduces the longer background action, so it takes the continuous.
  • He didn’t broke his leg. → He didn’t break his leg.After did / didn’t the main verb returns to the base form.
  • When I arrived, he already left. → When I arrived, he had already left.An event before the main past time needs the past perfect.
  • He had fallen into a stream and had broken his leg. → He fell into a stream and broke his leg.Told in order, these need only the past simple.
  • I was knowing the way. → I knew the way.Know is a state verb and takes no continuous.
  • Where you did go? → Where did you go?In questions, only the auxiliary moves in front of the subject.

More examples in context

  • event chainShe opened the door, looked inside and closed it again.
  • backgroundIt was raining hard when we set off.
  • interruptionI was writing the email when the power went off.
  • two long actionsHe was cooking while she was unpacking.
  • earlier eventBy the time the ambulance came, he had lost a lot of blood.
  • explaining a causeShe couldn’t pay because she had left her wallet at home.
  • state in the pastNobody knew where he was.
  • past perfect + alreadyThe film had already started when we sat down.
  • negativeThey didn’t realize he was missing until the evening.
  • questionHad you ever been there before that trip?

A tip for remembering it

Draw the story as a line. Events that move the story forward sit on the line in the past simple. A wavy line under an event is the past continuous — it started earlier and was still going. Anything you have to draw behind the line, before the story reached that point, is the past perfect.

Before you practise — the key rules

  1. Past simple = the events of the story, in order.
  2. Past continuous = a longer action already in progress, often interrupted by a past simple event.
  3. Past perfect = an event that happened before the point the story has reached.
  4. Use the past perfect only when the order is not already clear from the sentence.
  5. After did / didn’t the main verb goes back to its base form.
  6. A finished time expression (yesterday, last week) always means the past simple, never the present perfect.
